expectations.text: Asks batched clarifying questions before publishing numbers, covering at least abuse pressure, region count, gateway/edge capability, and deadline or effort ceiling
expectations.evidence: Open questions come after the policy, not before. They cover abuse, regions and gateway, but no deadline; Q5 only mentions 'engineering budget is tight'.

expectations.text: Rejects a single 300 req/min limit shared across REST and GraphQL: REST is metered by request counting and GraphQL by cost points, as two separately published models
expectations.evidence: '"300 requests/min covering both surfaces" doesn't work.' Requests for REST, cost points for GraphQL.

expectations.text: Expresses the GraphQL limit as a budget of cost points per window with a published cost formula, not a request count
expectations.evidence: 'GraphQL cost formula' with root 1, connection ceil(first÷100), mutation 5; worked example gives 12 points.

expectations.text: States explicitly whether the REST and GraphQL limits share anything (such as a common concurrency cap) instead of leaving the relationship between the two surfaces unstated
expectations.evidence: 'separate budgets... They share only the concurrency cap in section 2.'

expectations.text: Publishes burst and sustained as two explicit numbers per tier, never one blended figure
expectations.evidence: Plan table has separate 'REST sustained' and 'REST burst (bucket depth)' rows, and the same for GraphQL.

expectations.text: Recommends token bucket as the default algorithm, mapping bucket depth to the burst number and refill rate to the sustained quota
expectations.evidence: 'The sustained rate is the refill rate. The burst allowance is the bucket depth.'

expectations.text: Frames limits as identity/auth-scope x endpoint-class x account-override, treating the plan-to-limit mapping as a deliberate choice rather than the automatic default
expectations.evidence: Plan multipliers are accepted as 'fine, with three conditions'. The identity x class x override framing is never stated.

expectations.text: States which identifier each tier is keyed on and changes it up the ladder (IP for anonymous callers, API key or org for paid tiers)
expectations.evidence: 'All limits are per organization' for every tier; no IP-keyed anonymous tier.

expectations.text: Carves expensive operations out of the general budget with per-endpoint-class limits instead of one account-wide number
expectations.evidence: 'Bulk/export class: bulk import, bulk export, and report generation each get their own bucket.'

expectations.text: States the geographic scope of the published limit (global vs per-region enforcement)
expectations.evidence: 'limits are global per organization, not per region.' It also asks to confirm this, in open question 3.

expectations.text: Labels the published numbers operational hints rather than an SLA, reserving in writing the right to lower limits for stability
expectations.evidence: 'A published limit is an operational hint, not an SLA'; 'We may lower any override'; emergency reductions reserved.

expectations.text: Structures the tier ladder so anonymous/free callers learn limits from headers, self-serve paid tiers get a documented exact-numbers table, and any enterprise tier gets a process rather than a public number
expectations.evidence: No anonymous tier. Free, Growth and Scale are in a table and Enterprise is 'By agreement', but the anonymous/header-learned rung is missing.
